stages.title: Advanced vocabulary and terminology
stages.hook: "Education is the basis of development": in Arabic the phrase is only three words. Which little grammar trick joins "basis" and "development"?
explain: Advanced vocabulary is often abstract and built from patterns. The pattern -iyya makes abstract nouns: dīmuqrāṭiyya (democracy), ḥurriyya (freedom). Verbal nouns (maṣdar) turn actions into concepts: tanmiya (development), himāya (protection), tarbiya (upbringing). Many terms are coined to translate scientific and political words.

The construct state, called iḍāfa, joins two nouns: asāsu t-tanmiya, "the basis of development". The first noun loses al- and any tanwīn, and the second noun is genitive. The whole phrase is definite if the second noun is definite.
Learn word families: ʿadl (justice), ʿadāla (justice as a value), ʿādil (just), ʿadāla ijtimāʿiyya (social justice). This is how you build the terminology needed in news, politics and economics.
stages.mnemonic: Iḍāfa: two nouns hold hands, and the first loses its "the".
sentences: Education is the basis of development.
Protecting the environment is a shared responsibility.

gq.q: In the iḍāfa "asāsu t-tanmiya", which noun loses al-?
gq.why: The first noun of a construct is never marked with al- or tanwīn.

gq.q: What does the suffix -iyya often create?
o: An abstract noun, such as ḥurriyya (freedom)
gq.why: -iyya makes abstract nouns from adjectives and nouns.

panel.q: How is "the school's director" said?
panel.why: The first noun drops al-; the second is definite and genitive.

panel.q: Why does the second noun in an iḍāfa take the genitive?
o: It is "possessed-by" and Arabic marks this with -i
panel.why: The genitive marks the second member of the construct.

panel.q: Explain what a word family such as ʿadl, ʿadāla and ʿādil shows about Arabic vocabulary.
panel.model: They share the root ʿ-d-l with a core idea of justice; different patterns give a noun, an abstract noun and an adjective.
panel.why: Arabic builds vocabulary by patterns on roots.

teach.model: Arabic builds abstract words with patterns like -iyya and verbal nouns. Two nouns can be joined in a construct called iḍāfa, where the first noun has no al-.

stages.title: Academic language
stages.hook: In an academic paper, the voice often disappears: "It was found that...". How does Arabic say this without naming a person?
explain: Academic Arabic prefers the passive and the verbal noun: ujriyat dirāsa (a study was carried out), ittakhadha qarār (a decision was taken). It names the study, not the person: tubayyinu n-natāʾiju anna ... "the results show that ...".

Typical elements of a research paper: mulakhkhaṣ (abstract), muqaddima (introduction), manhaj (method), natāʾij (results), munāqasha (discussion), khātima (conclusion) and maṣādir (sources). Use anna with an accusative subject: tubayyinu d-dirāsatu anna l-qirāʾata tuḥassinu l-fahma.
Hedging softens claims: qad (may), yumkin (it is possible), ghāliban (often), tushīru ilā (points to). Academic writers avoid dialect and personal tone, and cite sources carefully.
stages.mnemonic: Academic Arabic: let the evidence speak, not "I".
sentences: The results of the study show that reading improves understanding.
The researcher relied on several sources.
We will analyse the data in the next section.

gq.q: Which word introduces the results section?
After "anna" (that), the subject is in which case?
gq.why: Anna, like inna, puts its subject in the accusative.

panel.q: Why is "ujriyat dirāsa" common in academic writing?
o: The passive focuses on the study, not the researcher
panel.why: The passive puts the research first and keeps a neutral tone.

panel.q: Which verb is best to hedge a claim?
panel.why: Qad + present makes the claim possible rather than certain.

panel.q: Name two features that make academic Arabic different from everyday speech.
panel.model: It uses formal MSA, passive and impersonal structures, precise terminology, hedging and citations of sources.
panel.why: Academic style is formal and impersonal.

teach.model: Academic writing uses MSA, the passive and abstract nouns. A paper has an abstract, method, results and conclusion. Hedging with qad keeps claims careful.

points.ask: What are the parts of a paper?
How do I make a careful claim?

stages.title: Professional communication
stages.hook: A formal email says "Please send the report before the deadline". What small word in Arabic turns this into a polite request instead of a command?
explain: Professional Arabic is formal and polite. Meetings are ijtimāʿ (pl. ijtimāʿāt) with a jadwal aʿmāl (agenda). A deadline is mawʿid nihāʾī. Contracts are ʿuqūd, a colleague is zamīl and a project is mashrūʿ. Salary is rātib.

Polite requests often use the passive with yurjā (it is requested): yurjā irsālu t-taqrīr, "please send the report". Thanks and announcements use naskuru-kum ʿalā taʿāwunikum and nawaddu iʿlāmakum bi-anna ..., "we would like to inform you that ...". Pronoun -kum is used for respect.

Business culture varies. Greetings and small talk usually come before business, and titles such as ustādh (Mr/teacher) or duktūr (doctor, also for PhD holders) are used. In many workplaces speakers move between MSA in writing and local dialect in meetings.
stages.mnemonic: Yurjā = "it is hoped": the polite way to ask.
sentences: The meeting will be held on Sunday morning.
Please send the report before the deadline.
We thank you for your cooperation.

gq.q: What does "yurjā" mean at the start of a request?
gq.why: Yurjā is a polite passive request.

gq.q: Which phrase starts "we would like to inform you"?
gq.why: Nawaddu iʿlāmakum is the standard opening.

panel.q: Why is "kum" used in "naskurukum" when writing to one manager?
o: It is a polite plural showing respect
panel.why: Using plural address for one person is a respect marker.

panel.q: An email begins with the dialect "ʿāyiz" (I want). Why is this inappropriate?
o: It is dialect and too direct for formal writing
It is wrong grammar in every dialect
It is a rude word in MSA only
panel.why: Formal communication uses MSA, with urīdu or yurjā.

panel.q: How would you make a request more polite in Arabic business writing?
panel.model: Use yurjā or min faḍlikum, the plural of respect (-kum), and thank the reader in advance.
panel.why: Politeness formulas are conventional.

teach.model: Professional Arabic uses polite passive forms like yurjā, the respectful plural -kum and thanks. Key words are ijtimāʿ for meeting, mawʿid nihāʾī for deadline and taqrīr for report.

stages.title: Literary analysis
stages.hook: A poet says the moon is "a lamp". Is that true, or is it something else? What do we call this?
explain: Arabic literary analysis uses terms from balāgha (rhetoric). Tashbīh is simile: "the moon is like a lamp". Istiʿāra is metaphor: the poet says "the moon is a lamp" without "like". Ṣūra (image) names the picture a text paints, and ramz is symbol. A narrator is the rāwī, the plot is ḥabka and style is uslūb.

Famous modern works: Naguib Mahfouz's Cairo Trilogy (Egypt), Tayeb Salih's Season of Migration to the North (Sudan), Ghassan Kanafani's Men in the Sun (Palestine) and the poems of Mahmoud Darwish (Palestine). Classical poems are studied for meter, rhyme and imagery.
Analysis steps: identify theme, narrator and setting; find images and symbols; explain their effect; support points with a quotation. Always separate what the text says from what you infer.
sentences: The poet compares the moon to a lamp.
The narrator tells the events in the first person.
Symbols give the text a deeper meaning.

gq.q: "The moon is a lamp" (without "like") is an example of:
gq.why: No word of comparison is used, so it is a metaphor.

gq.q: Who wrote "Season of Migration to the North"?
gq.why: It is a novel by the Sudanese writer Tayeb Salih.

panel.q: "Her face is like the moon" differs from "her face is the moon" because:
o: The first is a simile with "like", the second a metaphor
panel.why: The marker of comparison decides the type.

panel.q: Why must an analysis quote the text?
o: To show the reader a poem
panel.why: Quotation anchors the interpretation.

panel.q: Choose a metaphor or symbol and explain what it might mean in a text.
panel.model: For example, the lamp stands for hope or knowledge in dark times, so the metaphor suggests that learning lights the way.
panel.why: Interpretation links an image to a meaning.

teach.model: Literary analysis uses terms like tashbīh for simile, istiʿāra for metaphor, rāwī for narrator and ramz for symbol. Name the device, explain its effect and quote the text.

points.ask: What is the difference between them?
What parts does a story have?
How do I prove my interpretation?

stages.title: Advanced listening comprehension
stages.hook: A news presenter reads fast and drops the last vowels of each sentence. How can a listener still follow?
explain: Broadcast news is read in MSA, at speed. In a pause (waqf) the final short vowel is dropped, so you hear ar-rajul, not ar-rajulu. Listen for signposts: khabar ʿājil (breaking news), bi-ḥasabi maṣādir (according to sources), fī l-athnāʾ (meanwhile), aʿlana (announced).

Active listening: predict from the topic, catch the key nouns and verbs first, and use question words (who, what, where, when). News often follows a pattern: the main fact, then details, then background. Names and numbers need special attention.

Outside the news you will hear dialects. Compare the same message in MSA and a dialect: the MSA "mādhā turīdu" becomes "ʿāyiz ēh" in Egyptian and "shū biddak" in Levantine. Recognising patterns helps you understand a new dialect.
stages.mnemonic: Hear the five questions: who, what, where, when, why.
sentences: The minister announced a new plan.
According to official sources, the meeting ended.
Our correspondent reports from the city.

gq.q: In a pause (waqf), what happens to the final short vowel?
gq.why: Pausal form omits the final short vowel.
Bi-ḥasabi introduces a source of information.

panel.q: Why do news items often cite "maṣādir" (sources)?
o: To show where the information came from
panel.why: Attribution is a key convention in reporting.

panel.q: You hear "ar-rajul" with no final vowel in a sentence-final position. Why?
o: It is the pausal form, so the last vowel is dropped
panel.why: At a pause speakers drop the final short vowel.

panel.q: Give two strategies for understanding a fast Arabic news bulletin.
panel.model: Predict from the topic, listen for key nouns, verbs, names and numbers, and replay or take short notes.
panel.why: Focused listening is a skill with clear steps.

teach.model: News Arabic is MSA read fast, with final vowels dropped at pauses. Listen for key words, names and numbers. Phrases like bi-ḥasabi maṣādir show the source.

points.ask: What kind of Arabic is it?
How do I know where the news comes from?

stages.title: Oral fluency and presentations
stages.hook: You must speak for three minutes with no notes. What phrases can give your talk shape and give you time to think?
explain: Fluent speaking uses discourse markers: ḥasanan (well), kamā dhakartu (as I mentioned), daʿūnī uwaḍḍiḥ (let me explain), an-nuqṭa al-ūlā (the first point), bi-ikhtiṣār (in short), bi-ʿibāra ukhrā (in other words), shukran li-ḥusni istimāʿikum (thank you for listening).

A good presentation has a clear opening (topic and plan), three points with examples, a conclusion and an invitation for questions: hal min asʾila? Practise out loud, record yourself and listen for long vowels, throat sounds and doubled consonants.
In formal talks use MSA; in a friendly setting speakers might add some dialect. Do not mix randomly: choose your register and keep it.
stages.mnemonic: Open, three points, close: the three-room talk.
sentences: Today I will talk about the importance of water.
In other words, time is a valuable resource.
Thank you for listening; are there any questions?

o: To hear pronunciation and pacing you cannot notice while speaking
To memorise a script word for word
gq.why: Recording shows errors you may not notice.

panel.q: A speaker uses the dialect for the introduction, MSA for the middle and dialect again for the end. What is the likely problem?
o: Register switching without a plan can seem inconsistent
MSA cannot be used in talks
panel.why: Choose one register for a formal talk.

panel.q: What does "bi-ikhtiṣār" signal?
panel.why: It means "in brief".

panel.q: List three parts of a good short talk.
panel.model: An opening, a few points with examples, and a conclusion that invites questions.
panel.why: Structure helps listeners follow.

teach.model: Use markers like ḥasanan, kamā dhakartu and bi-ikhtiṣār to structure your speech. Open with the topic, give three points with examples, then close and invite questions.

points.ask: What phrases help structure a talk?

stages.title: Translation and interpretation
stages.hook: An interpreter hears a speech in Arabic and speaks English a few seconds later. How is that different from a translator?
explain: A translator works with written texts (tarjama), while an interpreter works with speech (tarjama shafawiyya or fawriyya). In consecutive interpreting the speaker pauses; in simultaneous interpreting the interpreter speaks almost at the same time, often through headphones.

Key concepts: al-lugha al-maṣdar (source language), al-lugha al-hadaf (target language), dirqa (accuracy), amāna (faithfulness), siyāq (context) and muṣṭalaḥ (term). Equivalence is not always one-to-one: "aʿtadhiru" is "I apologise", but "ma-ʿlīsh" is a dialect softener that needs different treatment.

Interpreters take notes, listen for ideas rather than words and manage culture: for example, in translation of "in shāʾ Allāh" the intended meaning (a sincere promise, a polite vagueness or a simple wish) depends on context and tone.
stages.mnemonic: Listen for ideas, not words; say the idea in the new language.
sentences: The interpreter translates the speech sentence by sentence.
Terminology must be precise and consistent.
The meaning depends on the context.

o: The speaker pauses so that the interpreter can speak
The interpreter speaks at the same time
gq.why: The interpreter waits for the speaker to finish a section.
The target is the language of the output.

panel.q: Why is a word-for-word interpreting of "in shāʾ Allāh" risky?
o: Its intention changes with context: a promise, a wish or polite vagueness
panel.why: Interpreters must convey function as well as form.

panel.q: Why does an interpreter note ideas rather than every word?
o: Memory holds ideas better and speech must keep pace
panel.why: Note-taking for interpreting uses symbols and keywords.

panel.q: Name one difference between translating and interpreting.
panel.model: Translators work with written text and have time to revise; interpreters work with live speech and must decide quickly.
panel.why: Medium and time pressure differ.

teach.model: Translators work with written text and interpreters with speech. The source language is what you hear; the target language is what you speak. Keep the meaning, context and tone.

stages.title: Idiomatic and figurative language
stages.hook: "One hand does not clap." What might this proverb teach, and how would you explain it to a friend in another language?
explain: Idioms and proverbs reveal culture. "Yad wāḥida lā tuṣaffiq" (one hand does not clap) teaches that cooperation is needed. "Ḥibr ʿalā waraq" (ink on paper) describes promises or rules that exist only on paper. "Qalbuhu abyaḍ" (his heart is white) means he is kind. "Khafīf ad-damm" (light of blood) means charming and witty; "thaqīl ad-damm" (heavy of blood) means annoying. These two are widely understood in Egyptian and Levantine speech.
Figurative language can also be lexical: ʿayn means eye, spring of water and spy. Context decides. When translating an idiom, look for an equivalent idiom or explain the meaning plainly.

Be careful with register. Many idioms are colloquial; avoid them in formal writing unless quoting. Say which dialect the idiom belongs to when you know it, for example "Allāh yaʿṭīka l-ʿāfiya", used to thank someone for their effort in Levantine and Gulf Arabic.
stages.mnemonic: Idioms are pictures: look at the picture, then say the meaning.
items: to kill two birds with one stone
thank you for your effort (Levantine and Gulf Arabic)
sentences: His heart is white and he is light of blood.
The promise remained ink on paper.

o: A promise or rule that exists only on paper
gq.why: It means something written but not carried out.

gq.q: The word ʿayn can mean eye, spring or spy. What decides the meaning?
gq.why: Context decides which sense of a polysemous word is meant.

panel.q: A translator renders "qalbuhu abyaḍ" as "his heart is the colour white". What is wrong?
o: The idiom means kind-hearted, so a literal translation misleads
panel.why: An idiom should be translated by meaning.

panel.q: Why should dialect idioms be labelled with their dialect?
o: Others may not understand them or may use different ones
Idioms do not exist in MSA
panel.why: Idioms are often regional.

panel.q: Explain what "yad wāḥida lā tuṣaffiq" teaches.
panel.model: One hand cannot clap: people need to cooperate to achieve things, because no one succeeds alone.
panel.why: It is a proverb about cooperation.

teach.model: Arabic idioms have figurative meanings, like ḥibr ʿalā waraq for an empty promise. Translate the meaning, not the words, and say which dialect you mean.

stages.title: Extended independent writing
stages.hook: An argumentative essay must convince. What would you write first: your opinion, or the opposite view?
explain: An extended essay has a thesis (uṭrūḥa), supporting arguments, a counter-argument and a conclusion. Opening formulas: min al-wāḍiḥ anna (it is clear that), lā yakhfā anna (it is undeniable that). Contrast: raghma (despite), baynamā (whereas), bi-l-muqābil (by contrast). Result: natījatan li-dhālika (as a result), wa-hākadhā (thus).

Questions guide an essay: ilā ayyi madā ...? (to what extent ...?). Develop each paragraph with one idea, an example and a link back to the thesis. Vary sentence types: nominal and verbal, short and long, active and passive.
Revise for agreement, case endings, connectors and register. Read aloud: Arabic prose has a rhythm, and awkward places are often clear to the ear. Keep a record of the sources you used.
stages.mnemonic: Thesis, proof, other side, answer, close: five steps.
sentences: It is clear that education changes society.
Despite the difficulties, the project succeeded.
Some prefer cities, whereas others prefer villages.

gq.q: In an argumentative essay, what does a counter-argument do?
o: Presents the opposite view and answers it
gq.why: It shows that you considered other positions.

panel.q: Which connector is best after a long list of reasons to show the result?
panel.why: It introduces a consequence.

panel.q: After "raghma" (despite), the next word is a noun in which case?
panel.why: Raghma is followed by a genitive noun, as in raghma aṣ-ṣuʿūbāt.

panel.q: Outline a five-part structure for an argumentative essay.
panel.model: Introduction with a thesis, supporting arguments with evidence, a counter-argument, a response to it, and a conclusion.
panel.why: A clear structure persuades.

teach.model: State a thesis, support it with arguments and examples, consider a counter-argument and finish with a conclusion. Use connectors such as raghma, baynamā and natījatan li-dhālika.
